tagline: Modes aren't an on/off allowlist — they're a **dial** for **how much Claude asks** before it acts.
summary: Claude Code runs in one of a handful of **permission modes**, and they form a **spectrum of autonomy** rather than a binary switch. At one end, **plan** mode proposes and acts on nothing. In the middle, **default** asks before risky actions and **acceptEdits** stops asking about file edits while still gating execution. Toward the far end, **dontAsk** and **auto** proceed with little or no prompting, and **bypassPermissions** removes the gate entirely. The mode doesn't change *what tools exist* — it changes **how often you're asked**.

sections.heading: A dial, not a toggle
body: The intuition that breaks is "permissions are an allowlist — a tool is either allowed or it isn't." The mode is better read as a **dial**: turn it down and Claude **asks about almost everything**; turn it up and it **asks about almost nothing**. Allowlists still exist, but the mode sets the **baseline posture**.
The same Agent and tool surface is available across modes. What shifts is the **friction**: how many actions stop to confirm with you first.

sections.heading: The stops along the dial
body: **plan** — Claude reasons and proposes; it does not edit, run, or change state. **default** — it asks before **risky** actions (writes, commands), acting freely only on safe reads. **acceptEdits** — it stops asking about ordinary **file edits**, but still **re-prompts before writes that grant code execution**.

**auto** — it runs autonomously, with a **classifier** still deciding what's safe to do unattended. **dontAsk** — it suppresses prompts and proceeds with **nothing in the way**. **bypassPermissions** — the gate is **removed**; nothing is asked. The exact rank of these high-autonomy modes is **approximate** — the direction, less and less asking, is the point.

sections.heading: Picking a point on the dial
body: The right mode is a function of **trust and blast radius**. Exploratory or destructive work wants a **low** setting (plan, default) where you stay in the loop. Repetitive, well-understood work tolerates a **high** setting (acceptEdits, auto) so you're not rubber-stamping every edit.

Two high settings are **not** the same: **auto** keeps a classifier in the loop deciding what's safe; **bypassPermissions** keeps **nothing** in the loop. Reaching for the highest setting by default is how people get surprised.

diagram.caption: The modes form a dial from **asks about everything** (plan) to **asks about nothing** (bypassPermissions). Turning it up trades confirmations for momentum.

nodes.label: plan — proposes, acts on nothing
nodes.note: The low end of the dial. Claude reasons and proposes a plan; it makes **no edits and runs nothing** until you approve.

nodes.label: default — asks before risky actions
nodes.note: Acts freely on safe reads, but **stops to confirm** writes and commands. The everyday balance point.

nodes.label: acceptEdits — auto-accepts edits
nodes.note: Stops asking about ordinary **file edits** — but still **re-prompts before writes that grant code execution** (shell rc files, build configs).

nodes.label: auto — autonomous, classifier-gated
nodes.note: Runs unattended, with a **classifier** deciding what's safe to do without asking. A **guard is still in the loop** — so it asks (and blocks) more than the modes past it.

nodes.label: dontAsk — suppresses prompts
nodes.note: Proceeds with **little prompting** and no classifier in the way. The exact rank of the high-autonomy modes is **approximate** — what matters is the direction.

nodes.label: bypassPermissions — no gate
nodes.note: The high end: the permission gate is **removed**. Nothing is asked. Maximum momentum, zero confirmation.

scenarios.title: Stay in the loop: **plan, then ease the dial up**
scenarios.note: Start where nothing happens without approval, then loosen to auto-accept edits once you trust the direction — still gated on execution-granting writes.

scenarios.title: Trade confirmations for momentum on trusted work
scenarios.note: Each step up removes a class of prompt. Note the gap between **auto** (a classifier still decides) and **dontAsk / bypass**, where less and less is judging.

misconceptions.myth: Permission modes are an allowlist — each tool is just on or off.
misconceptions.reality: Modes are a **graduated dial** for how much Claude asks before acting. They set the baseline posture; allowlists are a separate, finer-grained layer.
misconceptions.why: "Permission" sounds binary. But the modes range from proposes-nothing (plan) to asks-nothing (bypass), with several stops between.

misconceptions.myth: acceptEdits means it never asks about anything again.
misconceptions.reality: acceptEdits auto-accepts **ordinary file edits**, but still **re-prompts before writes that grant code execution** — shell startup files, build-tool configs.
misconceptions.why: "Accept edits" reads as total. The carve-out exists because some edits are really a way to run arbitrary code on the next shell or build.

misconceptions.myth: auto and bypassPermissions are the same "do anything" mode.
misconceptions.reality: **bypassPermissions** removes the gate entirely — nothing is consulted. **auto** keeps a **classifier** in the loop deciding what's safe to do unattended.
misconceptions.why: Both feel like "full autonomy," so they blur. The difference is whether *anything* is still judging each action — and that difference is the whole safety margin.
